catalog_quote: The syllable is defined as a unit of tone placement. Each syllable therefore has only one mora of length, a feature of the toneme; and a single vowel as its peak. ... The phonological phrase may contain one or more words and is a unit having one stress, whose placement is determined by the nucleus of falling and/or high tones as described in Section 3.1. ... High tone will be represented by an acute accent ( ') over the vowel, falling tone by a caret ... over the vowel, and low tone will be unmarked. ... In phonetic transcription only, stress will be marked by double quotation marks (") preceding the stressed syllable. In phonemic transcription stress being subphonemic will be unmarked. ... [ch. XIII, 3.2 Prosodic Features:] Both solutions require three degrees of pitch or three contrastive tones. Each syllable peak contains one of the three pitch features, high ( '), low (unmarked), an…

sources.note: The record's locator points to sec. 3.1 for the actual stress-placement rule but the held Rosetta excerpt lacked pp. 192-194; the full chapter (now downloaded) supplies the explicit tone-conditioned stress algorithm and the one-H-nucleus-per-word/phrase constraint, so the the primary-stress rule can be made exact and the domain note tightened.

sources.citation: Bee, Darlene. 1973. Usarufa: A Descriptive Grammar. In H. McKaughan (ed.), The Languages of the Eastern Family of the East New Guinea Highland Stock, 225-323. Seattle: University of Washington Press. Scan bundled in Bird (2011) LanguageCommons item (50 scan pages, 2-up).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 229: phoneme classes are defined by position in the 'stress group'; 'Tone is distinctive with high, low, and falling contrasts. For greater detail of both tone and segmental phonemes see Chapters XII and XIII.' p. 230: every nominal stem belongs to one of two tone classes and every verb stem to one of three tone classes, which determine tone sandhi. p. 234: '(There is one and only one nucleus of high tones within a single word and/or descriptive phrase.)' No independent word-stress rule is stated.
sources.locator: sec. 1.1 'Phonology and Orthography', p. 229; sec. 1.2 'Morphophonemics', p. 230; sec. 2.1.1.1, p. 234

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Re-records Bee & Glasgow's sec. 3.1 stress-conditioning examples and the tonal minimal sets; observes 'High tone is lowered after low', 'The evidence for a distinction between high and falling tone is scant. No minimal pairs exist (the closest is póma vs pûma)', and 'all Usarufa words must have at least one high tone'. No new stress analysis; treats the system as tonal with downtrend.
sources.locator: sections 'Recordings from Published Work' (3.1 Conditioning of Stress re-recorded) and 'Tone Transcription'
